newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Prodi defends budget, says no risk of vote.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Prodi defends budget, says no risk of vote.

text.p: Prime Minister Romano Prodi on Saturday defended his controversial 1997 budget and said there was no risk of an early general election over differences within his coalition about how to institute constitutional reform.
Prodi, in interviews published in two newspapers, said he was "very sure" parliament would approve his budget plan, which aims to cut 62.5 trillion lire ($42 billion) from Italy's huge public debt.
He told Corriere della Sera that in the end, people would understand that the tough budget measures were necessary if Italy wanted to join the planned European Union single currency.

A final vote on the budget is expected by mid-November in the Chamber of Deputies (lower house), where Prodi's centre-left coalition depends on the support of the hard-left Communist Refoundation. It then passes to the Senate, where coalition parties have a majority.
When asked by the interviewer why the government increased deficit-cutting measures from an expected 32 trillion lire to more than 62 trillion, Prodi replied:
"At first, the race towards Europe seemed slower. When it became clear that Germany and France were accelerating, there was no choice but for Italy to accelerate, too".

Prodi's budget, which is weighted heavily with new revenue-raising schemes, has been criticsised by employers' federations for largely avoiding a structural overhaul of welfare spending. Bank of Italy governor Antonio Fazio last week also said the government should concentrate efforts on structural spending cuts.
Prodi, while acknowledging that the pension system needed reform, said he felt these changes would be better made in future budgets.
"It would be easy to govern if you think of people only as numbers in a computer," he said. "We have to enter Europe without killing the people."
In an interview with Il Messaggero newspaper, Prodi was asked about a controversy with the largest party in his coalition over how to institute constitutional reform.

Massimo D'Alema, leader of the former communist Democratic Party of the Left, had warned last week that Italy faced political instability without a decisive push toward reform of Italy's electoral and parliamentary systems.
Parties within Prodi's coalition have been divided over what type of reform is needed.
Prodi told Il Messagero that issue would not lead to the downfall of his government. "There is no risk of elections."

Referring to the bus he used to criss-cross Italy during his election campaign last spring, Prodi said: "The bus is in a garage where it is resting. In my opinion, it will remain there. We will not need it".
